transcript.text: hotpoint SA2 oven not heatin on fan, grill ok. wat does SA2 mean??

The SA2 in Hotpoint model numbers typically refers to the specific oven cavity configuration and control layout. Here’s what it generally means:

• S: Often denotes a standard or single oven (as opposed to double ovens).
• A: Usually indicates an electric oven with a fan-assisted main oven.
• 2: Typically refers to the version or generation of that model, including control style, energy rating, or minor design updates.

In your case, since you have a fan oven that isn’t heating, but the grill works fine, this points to an issue with the fan heater element (also called the fan assist element), not the main baking element or the grill circuit.

### Why the Fan Oven Isn’t Heating:
1. Fan Heater Element Failure: The most common cause. This is a separate heating coil located behind the back panel of the oven, surrounding the fan. If it fails, the fan may still spin (you might hear it running), but no heat will be produced.
2. Thermal Fuse or Thermostat Issue: A blown thermal fuse or faulty thermostat can cut power to the fan element for safety reasons.
3. Control Board/Electronic Fault: Less common, but a fault in the electronic control module could prevent power from reaching the fan heater.

### What You Can Do:
1. Check if the fan spins: If you turn on the fan oven setting and hear the fan running but feel no heat after 5–10 minutes, the fan heater element is likely faulty.
2. Visual Inspection (Power Off!): Disconnect the oven from the mains. Remove the back panel inside the oven to inspect the fan heater element for visible breaks, burns, or discoloration.
3. Test with a Multimeter: If you’re comfortable doing so, test the resistance of the fan heater element. A reading of infinity (open circuit) means it’s broken and needs replacement.
4. Call a Qualified Engineer: Since this involves high-voltage appliances, it’s safest to have a Gas Safe or NICEIC-approved engineer diagnose and replace the part if needed.

### Summary:
SA2 = Standard Electric Fan-Assisted Oven (Model Variant 2)
Your issue is almost certainly a failed fan heater element. Replacement parts are usually available for Hotpoint models, but professional installation is recommended due to safety and warranty concerns.

The symptoms you’re describing — no heat on the fan oven setting, the fan not spinning (just a low hum), and prior noise from the same area — strongly suggest an issue with the fan motor or its associated components, rather than just the heating element. Here’s why:

Here is the complete explanation and a step-by-step guide on what to check next.

### Why it’s likely not just the heating element:
The main baking element (the U-shaped one at the bottom) only heats up; it does not drive the fan. If that were broken, the fan would still spin, but you wouldn’t get even heat or a roast function. Since the fan is silent (except for a hum), the problem is in the mechanical rotation part of the system: either the fan motor, the fan blade, or an electrical fault preventing the motor from starting.

The "low hum" you hear is actually a very important clue. It usually means electricity is reaching the motor, but something is physically stopping it from turning (a seized bearing) or the motor’s start capacitor has failed.

### What to check next (Safety First!)
⚠️ CRITICAL WARNING: Before doing anything inside the oven, you must isolate the appliance at the main fuse box/consumer unit. Do not just turn off the switch on the wall. Electric ovens carry lethal voltages even when switched off if accessed incorrectly.

#### Step 1: Check for a Stuck Fan Blade (Most Common & Easiest Fix)
Over time, baked-on grease and carbon can harden around the fan blade hub or in the motor bearings, causing it to seize. The "noisy for a few weeks" you mentioned is classic evidence of this gradual seizing process.

1.  Isolate power at the mains.
2.  Remove the back panel inside the oven (usually held by 4–6 screws). Note: On some Hotpoint SA models, the fan blade pulls straight off once the center nut is removed.
3.  Try to spin the fan blade by hand.
• If it feels stiff or won’t turn: This confirms a seized bearing or blocked hub. You may be able to free it with careful cleaning (using oven cleaner and a brush, then wiping thoroughly), but often the motor itself needs replacing if the bearings are shot.
• If it spins freely by hand: The problem is electrical (see Step 2).

#### Step 2: Check the Fan Motor Electrical Connections
If the fan spins freely by hand but doesn’t run when powered:

1.  With power still OFF, locate the motor at the back of the oven cavity.
2.  Check the wiring connections to the motor terminals. Ensure they are tight and not corroded or burnt. A loose connection can cause arcing (which might have caused the hum/noise) but prevent proper operation.
3.  Look for any signs of burning/melting on the wires near the motor.

#### Step 3: Test the Fan Motor (Requires Multimeter)
If connections are good and the blade spins freely, the motor itself is likely faulty.

1.  Disconnect the wires from the motor terminals.
2.  Use a multimeter set to Ohms (Ω).
3.  Place probes on the two main power terminals of the motor (ignore any small earth/ground wire terminal for now).
• Good reading: Typically between 50–150 Ω (varies by model). If you get "OL" or infinity, the internal windings are open-circuit and the motor is dead.
• Short circuit: If you get near 0 Ω, it’s shorted (also bad).
4.  Also check for continuity between each terminal and the metal casing of the motor. It should be infinite (no connection). If there’s continuity here, the motor has an earth fault and must be replaced immediately.

#### Step 4: Check the Capacitor (If applicable)
Some fan motors have a small external capacitor to help start rotation. If this fails, you might get a hum but no spin. It’s less common on newer Hotpoint SA models to have a separate user-replaceable cap, but it’s worth checking if your model has one attached near the motor terminals.

### Summary of Likely Causes:
1.  Seized Fan Motor Bearings: Very likely given the prior noise. The motor tries to turn but can’t, causing a hum and tripping thermal protection or just failing to start. (Most Common)
2.  Failed Fan Motor Windings: The internal electrical coil has burned out.
3.  Faulty Start Capacitor: Prevents the motor from getting the initial torque to spin.

### Recommendation:
Given your description, replace the entire fan motor assembly. It’s rarely worth trying to repair a seized motor because:
• The bearings are usually sealed and not serviceable.
• Cleaning baked-on grease is difficult and often doesn’t restore smooth operation long-term.
• A new motor is relatively inexpensive (£20–£40) compared to the risk of further electrical issues.

Next Action:
1.  Isolate power.
2.  Remove back panel.
3.  Try spinning the fan by hand. If stiff, replace motor. If free, test resistance with multimeter. If out of spec, replace motor.

If you are not comfortable working with high-voltage appliances or disassembling the oven, please contact a qualified appliance repair technician.
ok did it, isolated at the cooker switch first. fan blade is very stiff n feels gritty when i turn it by hand. also had a slight hot smell from the back once, not now. so is it the motor then?

That "gritty" feeling and stiffness confirm that the fan bearings are seized due to baked-on grease or carbon buildup. The previous noise was the motor struggling against this resistance, and the hot smell was likely the motor overheating as it tried to turn.

Since the blade is physically stuck, replacing just the heating element won’t fix the problem—the new element would also fail if the fan can’t spin. You need to address the mechanical blockage first.

Here are your options:

### Option 1: Clean and Free the Fan (The "DIY" Route)
If you want to try saving the existing motor, you must thoroughly clean the hub where the blade attaches to the motor shaft.
• How: Remove the fan blade completely. Use a stiff brush and oven cleaner on the metal hub and the motor spindle. Let it sit for 15–20 minutes, then scrub until the grit is gone. The blade should spin freely by hand afterward.
• Risk: If the bearings inside the motor housing are already worn out (which they likely are if it was noisy for weeks), cleaning might only buy you a few months before it seizes again.

### Option 2: Replace the Fan Motor Assembly (The "Proper" Fix)
This is the most reliable solution. You will need to replace the entire fan motor unit, which includes the new bearings and usually comes with a fresh fan blade.
• Part Name: Look for the "Fan Heater Element & Motor Assembly." Even though your heating element might still be okay, these are often sold as one combined unit on Hotpoint models like the SA2.
• Cost: These parts typically range from £40 to £80 depending on whether you buy an original Hotpoint part or a compatible aftermarket version.

### Next Steps:
1.  Find your exact model number: It will be on a sticker inside the oven door frame or on the side of the oven cavity (e.g., HT25.3B, etc.). The "SA2" is just the type; you need the full code to get the right motor.
2.  Order the part: Search for "[Your Full Model Number] fan heater element and motor."
3.  Installation: Once isolated at the mains, remove the back panel, disconnect the wires from the old motor (take a photo first!), unscrew the bracket holding it in place, and fit the new one.

If you aren't comfortable working with high-voltage appliances or disassembling the oven cavity, I strongly recommend calling a qualified engineer to handle this replacement.
found it on the rating plate in the door frame, its SA2 540 H IX. so which part do i order, just the fan motor?

For your Hotpoint model SA2 540 H IX, you should look for a "Fan Heater Element and Motor Assembly."

On this specific type of oven, the electric heating coil is permanently fixed to the back of the fan motor housing. You generally cannot buy them separately because they are designed as one single unit that bolts into the back wall of the oven cavity.

### What to search for:
• Part Name: Fan Heater Element and Motor Assembly (for Hotpoint SA2 540 H IX)
• Key Feature: Ensure it includes the fan blade. Most come with a new black plastic blade, which is much better than trying to clean your old gritty one.

### Why not just the motor?
If you were to find a bare motor (which is rare for this model), you would still have to deal with the old heating element that’s likely covered in years of baked-on grease. Replacing the whole assembly ensures both the mechanical part (the fan) and the electrical heating part are brand new.

### A quick note on your "gritty" fan:
Since you’ve already confirmed the old one is seized, do not try to force it or use excessive force to get it off. The plastic mounting clips can break easily if the motor has been stuck for a while. If it’s really tight, a little penetrating oil (like WD-40) on the shaft where it meets the blade might help loosen it before you pull.

Once you have the new assembly:
1.  Isolate power at the mains again.
2.  Unscrew the old unit from the back of the oven.
3.  Disconnect the wires (take a photo first so you know which goes where).
4.  Fit the new one, reconnect the wires, and test it.
